title: Four proposals, one an executive would actually fund
intro:
*Five minutes. Commit before you look.*

Four one-page proposals from internal communications leads to their executive sponsors. All four are competently written, all four ask for something reasonable, and all four are based on real work.

**One of them would get funded.** Find it.

Don't ask which is most ambitious or which sounds most strategic. Ask what the reader has to take on faith, and what the proposal is giving up.

artifacts.label: Proposal A
artifacts.body: "Internal communications should own AI adoption communications across the enterprise. AI is reshaping how our people work, and communication is central to successful adoption. We propose leading the communication strategy for all AI initiatives, partnering closely with IT and HR. **Ask:** two additional headcount and a tooling budget of £40k. **Success:** improved employee understanding of and confidence in our AI programme, measured through the annual engagement survey."

artifacts.label: Proposal B
artifacts.body:
"We mapped our function against the six stages of communication work. **68% of our time sits in production; 80% of our budget sits in the distribution platform; we have no owner and no budget line for listening or verification.** Meanwhile 45% of comms functions are already carrying AI rollout communication, and we are one of them — informally, unfunded, since March.

**Ask:** the AI adoption communication mandate, formally scoped, with the manager-enablement half named as ours and tooling decisions staying with IT.

**Baseline:** we sent this audience 31 separate communications in 30 days, costing an estimated 940 person-hours of attention. **At 90 days:** that figure, plus help-desk ticket volume on AI topics, plus the proportion of managers who report using our enablement material unchanged.

**To fund it we will stop** the weekly project-milestone digest, the quarterly all-staff newsletter, and the standalone system-notice channel — returning roughly 310 person-hours a month and about 6 hours a week of my team's capacity."

artifacts.label: Proposal C
artifacts.body:
"Our analysis shows employees are anxious about AI, and anxiety is a communication problem. We propose a comprehensive AI communication programme: a monthly AI newsletter, a dedicated intranet hub, a quarterly town hall series, an AI champions network across all sites, and a manager toolkit refreshed each quarter.

**Ask:** £120k and one FTE. **Success:** 80% employee awareness of our AI strategy within six months, measured by pulse survey."

artifacts.label: Proposal D
artifacts.body:
"Having mapped our function and audited our output, **we recommend against claiming the AI adoption mandate.** Our compression map shows 71% of time in production with no verification owner; taking on a new mandate before fixing that would mean carrying enterprise-critical communication on a function that cannot currently verify its own output.

**Instead we propose** owning AI adoption communication from Q3, conditional on two things landing first: a named verification owner, and the manager-enablement pilot completing. **We will stop** the milestone digest now to fund the verification role from existing budget. **At 90 days** we will report whether the pilot changed manager-reported confidence, and decide then."

reasoning:
**B is the one, and every element is doing work.**

The mandate is **scoped tightly enough to be refused** — manager enablement named as theirs, tooling decisions explicitly left with IT. A sponsor can say yes to that without wondering what they've just agreed to, which is the property most proposals lack.

The evidence is **theirs and nobody else's**. The 68%/80% line is the compression map doing exactly what Module 4 said it would: the time is in the collapsing link, the money is in the solved one, and nothing at all is aimed at the links that would tell you whether any of it works. No sponsor has seen that analysis of their own communications function before, because almost nobody draws it.

The baseline is **a real number with a real date**, not an aspiration. And the 90-day measure comes from the families that pass Module 3's test — ticket volume and manager-reported use would both change what the team does next week. Contrast with A and C, which measure awareness on an annual or six-monthly survey and therefore cannot fail in a way that produces an action.

And then the line that closes it: **three named things stopped, with the returned capacity quantified in both currencies** — the workforce's attention and the team's hours. That is what converts a request into a trade, and it is the sentence an executive is actually reading for.

One more thing worth noticing: **"we are one of them — informally, unfunded, since March"** reframes the ask entirely. It is not a request for new territory. It is a request to formalize something already happening, which is a far smaller decision for a sponsor to make.

**A is the most common shape and the least fundable.** "Own AI adoption communications across the enterprise" cannot be refused because it cannot be pinned down, the success measure is annual and unfalsifiable, and it asks for two heads while giving up nothing.

**C is a plan, not a bet.** Five workstreams, all additive, no baseline, and a success measure — 80% awareness — that is both unverifiable and beside the point. It also fails this track's own argument in an obvious way: the response to an over-communicated workforce is a newsletter, a hub, a town hall series and a champions network.

**D is the strongest of the three losers and worth taking seriously.** It has evidence, a stop, a condition and a decision date — and in some organizations it is genuinely the right answer, which is why the activity accepts a well-argued refusal at full credit. It loses to B only on timing: it defers a mandate that is being assigned *now*, and "we'll take it in Q3" is how a function watches something land somewhere else in Q2.
